items.title: Q1 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Geoffrey Hartman, Roland Barthes, Michel Foucault, Harold Bloom, Julia Kristeva
items.stem: Identify the one that has not been paired correctly.
options: Criticism in the Wilderness - Geoffrey Hartman
items.explanation: Madness and Civilization: A History of Insanity in the Age of Reason (1961) was written by French philosopher Michel Foucault, not Roland Barthes. Criticism in the Wilderness (1980) is by Geoffrey Hartman, Poetry and Repression (1976) is by Harold Bloom, and Strangers to Ourselves (1988) is by Julia Kristeva.

items.title: Q2 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution made the provision for use of English, alongside Hindi, for official purposes, for fifteen years?
items.explanation: Article 343(2) of the Constitution of India declared Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union while providing that the English language should continue to be used for all official purposes of the Union for a period of fifteen years (until 1965).

items.title: Q3 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: What is meant by "Corporate author" in research?
options: A writer who belongs to a corporate company
A writer who writes on matters of corporate affairs
A work produced by an institution, an association or a government agency
items.explanation: In research methodology and bibliographic citation (such as MLA style), a 'corporate author' refers to an institution, commission, association, corporation, or government agency that produces a work in its collective name without attributing it to an individual personal author.

items.title: Q4 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roman Jakobson, Ferdinand de Saussure, Roland Barthes, J. L. Austin
items.stem: Which of the following theorists identifies "metonymy" and "metaphor" as two fundamental structures of language?
items.explanation: In his landmark 1956 essay 'Two Aspects of Language and Two Types of Aphasic Disturbances', Russian-American structuralist linguist Roman Jakobson identified metaphor (operating on the paradigmatic axis of selection and similarity) and metonymy (operating on the syntagmatic axis of combination and contiguity) as the two fundamental poles of language.

items.title: Q5 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: Which of the following is not true about "Lyrical Ballads"?
options: It is a manifesto of Romantic poetry
It turns English Poetry away from the social and intellectual sophistication of the seventeenth and the eighteenth century poetry
It takes poetry out of the confines of reason and intellect to the unravished and unspoilt beauties of nature
It is very particular about the form and structure of a poem
items.explanation: William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798, with the 1800 'Preface') was an experimental collection that rejected rigid neoclassical rules of poetic diction and formal structure in favour of natural speech, rustic life, and spontaneous emotion.

items.title: Q6 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · J. Hillis Miller, Percy Bysshe Shelley
items.stem: J. Hillis Miller, one of the leading exponents of deconstruction, makes a deconstructionist reading of which of the following poems of P. B. Shelley?
items.explanation: Yale School critic J. Hillis Miller's influential essay 'The Critic as Host' and his contribution to Deconstruction and Criticism (1979)—a volume centered on deconstructive readings of Percy Bysshe Shelley's unfinished final poem 'The Triumph of Life'—examine Shelley's 'The Triumph of Life'.

items.title: Q7 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: The Deserted Village by Oliver Goldsmith
options: Voices revolt of the individual man against institutions
Reflects upon different views on the human soul
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith's pastoral elegiac poem The Deserted Village (1770) laments the depopulation of rural 'Sweet Auburn' through land enclosure and commercial greed, voicing the individual's protest against oppressive socio-economic institutions.

items.title: Q8 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Alfred Lord Tennyson
items.stem:
A. L. Tennyson in the following lines :
"Yet I doubt not through the ages one increasing purpose runs,
And the thoughts of men are widen'd with the process of the suns"
items.explanation: These lines from Alfred Lord Tennyson's 'Locksley Hall' (1842) express Victorian evolutionary faith—the belief that human thought and history progressively advance toward a higher teleological purpose over time.

items.title: Q9 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Philip Sidney's Arcadia was influenced by
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney's Elizabethan pastoral prose romance Arcadia (composed c. 1580, published 1590/1593) was directly influenced by Jorge de Montemayor's Spanish pastoral romance Los siete libros de la Diana (1559), as well as Jacopo Sannazaro's Italian Arcadia and Heliodorus's Aethiopica.

items.title: Q10 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Cyril Tourneur, Thomas Middleton
items.stem: Who among the following has authored The Revenger's Tragedie?
items.explanation: The Jacobean revenge play The Revenger's Tragedy (published anonymously in 1607) was traditionally attributed to Cyril Tourneur, though modern scholarship since the late twentieth century generally assigns it to Thomas Middleton.

items.title: Q11 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry · George Chapman
items.stem: Besides being a playwright, who among the following has translated Homer?
items.explanation: Elizabethan dramatist and poet George Chapman (c. 1559–1634) famously translated Homer's Iliad (in fourteeners, completed 1611) and Odyssey (in heroic couplets, 1616), later celebrated in John Keats's sonnet 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer'.

items.title: Q12 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Who among the following in the article, "Fleshly School of Poetry", attacked the Pre-Raphaelites, especially D. G. Rossetti?
items.explanation: Scottish poet and critic Robert Williams Buchanan published the polemical article 'The Fleshly School of Poetry' in The Contemporary Review (October 1871) under the pseudonym Thomas Maitland, attacking Dante Gabriel Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelites for sensualism.

items.title: Q13 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Percy Bysshe Shelley
items.stem: Which among the following is an incomplete poem by P. B. Shelley?
items.explanation: 'The Triumph of Life' (composed in terza rima in the spring and summer of 1822 and published posthumously by Mary Shelley in Posthumous Poems, 1824) was left incomplete when Percy Bysshe Shelley drowned in the Gulf of Spezia on 8 July 1822.

items.title: Q14 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Who among the following attached himself to the Earl of Nottingham's theatrical company?
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe attached himself to the Lord Admiral's (Earl of Nottingham's) theatrical company, managed by Philip Henslowe and led by actor Edward Alleyn, which staged Tamburlaine, Doctor Faustus, and The Jew of Malta.

items.title: Q15 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Haruki Murakami
items.stem: When was Haruki Murakami's Men Without Women published?
items.explanation: Japanese writer Haruki Murakami's short story collection Men Without Women (Onna no inai otokotachi) was first published in Japan on 18 April 2014 (Option 3), and its English translation by Philip Gabriel and Ted Goossen was published in May 2017 (Option 1).

items.title: Q16 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Ania Loomba, Meenakshi Mukherjee
items.stem: Who is the author of the essay "Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism" (1985)?
items.explanation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak wrote the influential postcolonial feminist essay 'Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism' (Critical Inquiry, 1985), analyzing Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre, Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.

items.title: Q17 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Chandra Talpade Mohanty, Karl Marx
items.stem:
Who among the following critics appropriates the following statement by Karl Marx?
"They cannot represent themselves : they must be represented".
items.explanation: Postcolonial feminist theorist Chandra Talpade Mohanty (alongside Edward Said in Orientalism and Spivak in 'Can the Subaltern Speak?') appropriates Karl Marx's line from The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte to critique Western feminism's homogenizing representation of Third World women.

items.title: Q18 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Iris Murdoch, John Fowles
items.stem: Under the Net (1954) is written by
items.explanation: Under the Net (1954) is the debut novel of Anglo-Irish philosopher and novelist Iris Murdoch, following struggling writer Jake Donaghue through picaresque and philosophical adventures across London and Paris.

items.title: Q19 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot, W. H. Auden
items.stem: Who among the following is not a recipient of the Nobel Prize for Literature?
items.explanation: Marie Curie (Madam Curie) won Nobel Prizes in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911), whereas T. S. Eliot (1948) and Winston Churchill (1953) won the Nobel Prize in Literature; W. H. Auden was also never awarded the Literature Nobel.

items.title: Q20 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · V. S. Naipaul
items.stem: Find out the correct sequence of the publications of the following books:
options: India : An Area of Darkness; India : A Wounded Civilization; India : A Million Mutinies Now; A House for Mr. Biswas
A House for Mr. Biswas; India : A Million Mutinies Now; India : An Area of Darkness; India : A Wounded Civilization
A House for Mr. Biswas; India : An Area of Darkness; India : A Wounded Civilization; India : A Million Mutinies Now
India : A Wounded Civilization; A House for Mr. Biswas; India : An Area of Darkness; India : A Million Mutinies Now
items.explanation: V. S. Naipaul's major works listed here appeared in the chronological order: A House for Mr Biswas (1961), An Area of Darkness (1964), India: A Wounded Civilization (1977), and India: A Million Mutinies Now (1990).

items.title: Q21 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The "Ancient and Modern Quarrel" in Western Literary Criticism appears during
items.explanation: The 'Quarrel of the Ancients and the Moderns' (Querelle des Anciens et des Modernes) emerged in Western literary criticism during the sixteenth-century Renaissance in Italy and France before culminating in late seventeenth-century French and English neoclassical debates (such as Swift's The Battle of the Books).

items.title: Q22 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Miles Coverdale
items.stem: In which year Miles Coverdale translated The Old Testament of The Bible?
items.explanation: English Reformation scholar Miles Coverdale produced the first complete printed English translation of the Bible (Biblia: The Bible, that is, the holy Scripture of the Olde and Newe Testament), translating the Old Testament in 1535.

items.title: Q23 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer, William Langland
items.stem: Who is the author of the poem "House of Fame"?
items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer composed the Middle English dream-vision poem The House of Fame (c. 1379–1380) in octosyllabic couplets, drawing on Ovid, Virgil's Aeneid, and Dante's Divine Comedy.

items.title: Q24 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit II: Poetry · John Dryden, Alexander Pope
items.stem: The heroic couplet is a pair of
options: Eight-syllable lines that do not rhyme
items.explanation: A heroic couplet consists of two rhyming lines of iambic pentameter (ten-syllable lines rhyming AA), perfected in English verse by Geoffrey Chaucer, John Dryden, and Alexander Pope.

items.title: Q25 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: The book Women Beware Women was published in the year
items.explanation: Thomas Middleton's Jacobean tragedy Women Beware Women is dated by dramatic historians to c. 1621 (though first printed posthumously in Two New Playes in 1657).

items.title: Q26 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Amitav Ghosh
items.stem: Which of the following is not a part of Amitav Ghosh's Ibis Trilogy?
items.explanation: Amitav Ghosh's Ibis Trilogy comprises Sea of Poppies (2008), River of Smoke (2011), and Flood of Fire (2015), whereas The Calcutta Chromosome (1995) is his standalone medical science-fiction thriller.

items.title: Q27 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Ernest Hemingway
items.stem: "A man can be destroyed but not defeated". Which of the following texts glorifies this as its predominant theme?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
items.explanation: In Ernest Hemingway's novella The Old Man and the Sea (1952), aging Cuban fisherman Santiago declares during his epic struggle with the giant marlin and sharks: 'But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.'

items.title: Q28 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Edward Said, Mikhail Bakhtin, Roland Barthes, Jacques Derrida
items.stem: Which of the following critics is associated with the term "contrapuntal reading"?
items.explanation: Edward Said introduced the concept of 'contrapuntal reading' in Culture and Imperialism (1993) to read canonical Western texts alongside the submerged histories of imperialism and anti-colonial resistance they take for granted.

items.title: Q29 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Elaine Showalter, Sandra Gilbert, Susan Gubar, Virginia Woolf
items.stem: Who is the author of A Literature of their Own?
items.explanation: American feminist critic Elaine Showalter authored A Literature of Their Own: British Women Novelists from Brontë to Lessing (1977), a foundational work of gynocriticism.

items.title: Q30 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Taylor Coleridge, William Wordsworth
items.stem: Who said, "There is, there can be and there ought to be the difference between the language of prose and metrical composition"?
items.explanation: In Chapter 18 of Biographia Literaria (1817), Samuel Taylor Coleridge refutes William Wordsworth's Preface to Lyrical Ballads by arguing that 'there is, there can be, and there ought to be' an essential difference between the language of prose and metrical composition.

items.title: Q31 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stuart Hall
items.stem: Stuart Hall belongs to __________ school of cultural studies.
items.explanation: Jamaican-born theorist Stuart Hall was a leading figure of the Birmingham School of Cultural Studies, serving as director of the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) at the University of Birmingham from 1968 to 1979.

items.title: Q32 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Tolkappiyam is a book of grammar and poetics written in the __________ language.
items.explanation: Tolkappiyam, attributed to Tolkappiyar, is the oldest extant treatise on Tamil grammar, phonology, syntax, and Sangam poetics (akam and puram conventions).

items.title: Q33 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Gaiutra Bahadur
items.stem: Gaiutra Bahadur wrote an autobiographic novel titled
items.explanation: Guyanese-American writer Gaiutra Bahadur authored Coolie Woman: The Odyssey of Indenture (2013), an autobiographical and historical account tracing her great-grandmother Sujaria's 1903 journey from colonial India to British Guiana.

items.title: Q34 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Subramani
items.stem: Subramani's Fantasy Eaters (1988) is a
items.explanation: Indo-Fijian writer and academic Subramani's The Fantasy Eaters: Stories from Fiji (1988) is a pioneering collection of short stories exploring the Girmitiya (indentured Indian) diaspora experience in Fiji.

items.title: Q35 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Canadian Multiculturalism Act was passed in the year :
items.explanation: The Canadian Multiculturalism Act, which gave statutory recognition to Canada's federal policy of cultural diversity and equality, was passed by Parliament in July 1988.

items.title: Q36 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · V. S. Naipaul
items.stem: The Writer and the World by V. S. Naipaul is a
items.explanation: The Writer and the World: Essays (2002), edited and introduced by Pankaj Mishra, is a comprehensive collection of V. S. Naipaul's essays and long-form reportage on India, Africa, the Caribbean diaspora, and America.

items.title: Q37 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Homi K. Bhabha, Salman Rushdie, Edward Said, Benedict Anderson
items.stem: "It is significant that the productive capacities of this Third Space have a colonial or postcolonial provenance". The above lines have been written by
items.explanation: Postcolonial theorist Homi K. Bhabha wrote this famous sentence on cultural hybridity and the 'Third Space of enunciation' in his essay 'The Commitment to Theory' in The Location of Culture (1994).

items.title: Q38 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida
items.stem: Find the correct explanation of the term "Aporia" :
options: It denotes a speaker's or character's deliberation on an irresolvable question
It is an address to something inanimate
It is applied to a work of art fraught with inherent tension
It refers to a form of denial of existence
items.explanation: In classical rhetoric and deconstruction (as used by Jacques Derrida), 'aporia' denotes an irresolvable internal contradiction, logical impasse, or a speaker's deliberation over an insoluble question.

items.title: Q39 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Seamus Heaney, John Osborne, Kingsley Amis, Philip Larkin
items.stem: Which writer does not belong to the Angry Young Men Movement?
items.explanation: Irish Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney was associated with the Northern Ireland Belfast Group rather than 1950s British 'Angry Young Men' and Movement writers like John Osborne, Kingsley Amis, and Philip Larkin.

items.title: Q40 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Kingsley Amis, Philip Larkin, Donald Davie, John Wain
items.stem:

Or squash it flat?
Man's love is of man's life a thing apart;

items.explanation: These witty, anti-romantic lines parodying Lord Byron's Don Juan appear in Kingsley Amis's Movement poem 'A Bookshop Idyll' from his collection A Case of Samples (1956).

items.title: Q41 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)

items.explanation: Articulate Silences (1970) was written by Shiv K. Kumar and A Time to Change (1952) by Nissim Ezekiel (B and E only), whereas Stone Roots (1980), River and Bridge (1995), and Raw Silk (2004) are poetry collections by Meena Alexander.

items.title: Q42 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of these are not forms of flash fiction?
A. Drabble
B. Postcard fiction
C. Novelette
D. Short Story
E. Nanofiction
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Drabble (exactly 100 words, A), postcard fiction (B), and nanofiction/microfiction (E) are all subgenres of flash fiction, whereas the novelette (C) and traditional short story (D) are longer narrative forms; among the printed options (which omitted 'C and D only'), NTA keyed Option 3 / Option 4.

items.title: Q43 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Matthew Arnold, W. H. Auden, Alfred Lord Tennyson
items.stem:
Identify the poems termed as "pastoral elegies" :
A. Lycidas
B. In Memory of W.B. Yeats
C. Adonais
D. Thyrsis
E. In Memoriam
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: John Milton's 'Lycidas' (1637), P. B. Shelley's Adonais (1821), and Matthew Arnold's 'Thyrsis' (1866) are classic English pastoral elegies (A, C and D only), unlike W. H. Auden's modernist elegy 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' or Tennyson's In Memoriam.

items.title: Q44 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Fyodor Dostoevsky
items.stem:
Identify the correct combination among the following :
A. Demons — Novel
B. Landlady — Novella
C. The Crocodile — Short-Story
D. A Writer's Diary — Essay
E. Mary Stuart — Translation
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Among Fyodor Dostoevsky's works, The Landlady (1847) is a novella (B), 'The Crocodile' (1865) is a satirical short story (C), and A Writer's Diary (1873–1881) consists of journalistic essays and sketches (D), giving Option 4 (B, C and D only).

items.title: Q45 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Arun Kolatkar, Dilip Chitre
items.stem:
Identify the correct ones among the following :
A. Arun Kolatkar uses colloquial speech in his poems
B. Kolatkar envisions abstract qualities to paint a picture of life of his own kind
C. The poem Boatride by Kolatkar talks about a ride in the Ganges
D. Private Poems in Public Garden is composed by Dilip Chitre
E. 'In Ethiopia' is a poem on Africa by Arun Kolatkar
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Arun Kolatkar is celebrated for his colloquial idiom (A), defamiliarizing visual imagery (B), and his long meditative sequence 'The Boatride' (C, though set off the Gateway of India in Bombay Harbour; Dilip Chitre wrote the Ethiopia poems in Travelling in a Cage, making E false and A, B and C the keyed combination).

items.title: Q46 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Doris Lessing
items.stem:
Which of these are correct combination of the works by Doris Lessing and their respective themes?
A. The Golden Notebook deals with Johor travelling to Rohonda
B. The Good Terrorist is about a doomed love affair
C. Shikasta is about a planet, which is cut-off due to the advanced influence of civilization
D. Alfred and Emily explores the life of her parents
E. The Grass is Singing draws from her experiences in Africa
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In Doris Lessing's oeuvre, Shikasta (1979) depicts the colonized planet Rohanda/Shikasta cut off from Canopus (C), Alfred and Emily (2008) reimagines her parents' lives (D), and The Grass Is Singing (1950) draws on her youth in Southern Rhodesia (E), making C, D and E correct.

items.title: Q47 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Identify the correct combination among the following :
A. Spondee : It consists of three stressed syllables
B. Pyrrhic : It consists of two unstressed syllables
C. Amphimacer : It is a metrical foot of three syllables
D. Choriambus : It is a foot of verse consisting of two stressed syllables enclosing two unstressed syllables
E. Trochaic : It has a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In English prosody, a spondee has two stressed syllables (making A false, since three stressed syllables form a molossus), whereas Pyrrhic (two unstressed, B), Amphimacer/cretic (three syllables: stressed-unstressed-stressed, C), Choriambus (stressed-unstressed-unstressed-stressed, D), and Trochaic (stressed-unstressed, E) are all accurately defined.

items.title: Q48 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roland Barthes
items.stem:
Which of the following observations are true about Roland Barthes' contributions to literary theory?
A. He rejected the model for structural analysis of narratives
B. He perceived "meaning" as an effect of various interconnections among linguistic codes
C. He identified the various codes found in the process of structuration
D. He played a significant role in the development of 'semiology'
E. He questioned the concept of literary criticism as an act of uncovering some hidden truth intended by the "Author"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: B, C, D and E only
A, B, C, D and E only
items.explanation: Roland Barthes pioneered semiology (D), analyzed narrative codes in S/Z (B, C), and challenged authorial intentionality in 'The Death of the Author' (E); statement A is false because he championed structural narrative analysis in 1966, making Option 3 (B, C, D and E only) correct.

items.title: Q49 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Keble, John Henry Newman
items.stem:
Which among the following is true about the Tractarian Movement?
A. It was widespread across the world
B. The other leaders of the movement were Paul Newman and R. H. Froude
C. The movement began with a sermon by John Keble in 1833
D. Pusey gave the movement cohesion, fame and a name
E. The ideal of the Christian Church was praised by Oxford Convocation
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: The Oxford (Tractarian) Movement began with John Keble's 1833 Assize Sermon 'National Apostasy' (C), was led by John Henry Newman and Richard Hurrell Froude (B), and gained cohesion and the name 'Puseyism' through Edward Bouverie Pusey (D), making Option 4 (B, C and D only) correct.

items.title: Q50 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Elaine Showalter
items.stem:

D. Feminist

items.explanation: In A Literature of Their Own (1977), Elaine Showalter divides the evolution of women's writing into three historical phases: the Feminine (1840–1880), the Feminist (1880–1920), and the Female (1920–present), corresponding to A, D and E only.

B. Saint Joan of Stockyards
C. Death of a Salesman
D. Candida

items.explanation: Capitalist greed and consumerism are central themes in Bertolt Brecht's Saint Joan of the Stockyards (1932), set in Chicago's meatpacking markets, and Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman (1949), critiquing the commodified American Dream (B and C only).

items.explanation: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) was developed by Richard Bandler and John Grinder in the 1970s (C), wherein 'Neuro' refers to how sensory experiences (A), invisible thoughts, and visible physiological reactions (D) shape human behaviour and communication (A, C and D only).

items.title: Q53 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Kimberle Crenshaw

Kimberle Crenshaw's term "intersectionality" is widely used for
A. academic deterioration
B. racial justice
C. peace formation
D. complex construction of power
E. identity politics
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw coined the term 'intersectionality' (1989) to analyze how overlapping social categorizations such as race, gender, and class create interlocking systems of discrimination and privilege, making it central to racial justice (B), the complex construction of power (D), and identity politics (E).

B. It advocates teaching of European texts and literature to the students of the third world countries
C. It reflects negatively upon the literature taught to the Kenyan students in National Schools
D. It argues that cultural imperialism distorts people's vision of history
E. It observes that European teachers are better equipped to teach literature to the Kenyan students
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In his essay 'Literature in Schools' (collected in Writers in Politics, 1981), Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o examines the relevance of the postcolonial education system (A), critiques the Eurocentric literature taught to Kenyan children in national schools (C), and argues that cultural imperialism distorts colonized people's understanding of their own history (D).

items.title: Q57 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Bhartrhari, Anandavardhana

Which of the following concepts are associated with Bhartrhari's theory of 'Sphota'?
A. Rasa
B. Alankara
C. Dhvani
D. Vakrokti
E. Shabda Brahman
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In the 5th-century Sanskrit grammarian Bhartrhari's Vakyapadiya, the philosophy of Sphota (the indivisible flash of linguistic meaning) is directly linked to Shabda-Brahman (ultimate reality as the eternal Word) and inspired Anandavardhana's theory of Dhvani (C and E only).

Which among the following are appropriate about Latin American Literature?

B. The Latin American Literary tradition draws analogy between plant growth and human movement
C. Dzul Poot's stories depict the geography of the Chilam Balam Towns
D. Quechua had a wider popularity and presence across different nations.
E. The Latin American Literature is unitary and refrains from intertextuality of any kind
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: As documented in Literary Cultures of Latin America, Mesoamerican indigenous literary traditions draw analogies between plant growth and human movement (B), Domingo Dzul Poot's Yucatec Maya tales depict the geography of the Chilam Balam towns (C), and Quechua enjoyed wide transnational presence across Andean nations (D), whereas Latin American literature is racially diverse and richly intertextual (making A and E false).

B. Proairetic code
C. Semic code
D. Hermeneutic code
E. Symbolic code
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: B, C, D and E only
items.explanation: In S/Z (1970), Roland Barthes identifies five narrative codes: Hermeneutic, Proairetic, Semic, Symbolic, and Cultural/Referential; thus B (Proairetic), C (Semic), D (Hermeneutic), and E (Symbolic) are authentic Barthesian codes (Option 4: B, C, D and E only).

items.title: Q63 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Aristotle
items.stem:
What does Aristotle mean by the phrase "language with pleasurable accessories" in his definition of tragedy?
A. A language full of pompous vocabulary
B. An embellished language
C. A language full of rhythm and harmony
D. A language superadded with song
E. Emotive language
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In Chapter VI of the Poetics, Aristotle explicitly defines 'language with pleasurable accessories' (or 'embellished language') as 'language into which rhythm, "harmony" [meter], and song enter'—that is, a language full of rhythm and harmony (C) and superadded with song (D).

items.explanation: Harold Pinter (born in 1930, making A false) was deeply influenced by Samuel Beckett and the Theatre of the Absurd (B), created the protagonist Stanley Webber in The Birthday Party (1957, D), and depicted a married couple's extramarital affair in reverse chronology in Betrayal (1978, E); The Alchemist is by Ben Jonson (making C false).

items.title: Q65 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Plato
items.stem:
Which of the following are Plato's main objections against poetry?
A. The poet is an imitator.
B. The poet is incapable of bravery.
C. The poet, by fueling passions and emotions, weakens the reasoning capacity of the citizens.
D. The poet is less responsible.
E. The poet has no knowledge of the world.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In the Republic (Books III and X), Plato objects to poetry because the poet is a mere imitator thrice removed from truth (A), fuels passions that weaken citizens' rational self-control (C), and lacks genuine knowledge of what he imitates (E), giving Option 1 (A, C and E only).

items.title: Q96 · Oct 2022 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin
items.stem:
Read the following poem, and answer the question that follows (96-100):

Mr Bleaney

'This was Mr Bleaney's room. He stayed
The whole time he was at the Bodies, till
They moved him.' Flowered curtains, thin and frayed,
Fall to within five inches of the sill,

Whose window shows a strip of building land,
Tussocky, littered. 'Mr Bleaney took
My bit of garden properly in hand.'
Bed, upright chair, sixty-watt bulb, no hook

Behind the door, no room for books or bags —
'I'll take it.' So it happens that I lie
Where Mr Bleaney lay, and stub my fags
On the same saucer-souvenir, and try

Stuffing my ears with cotton-wool, to drown
The jabbering set he egged her on to buy.
I know his habits — what time he came down,
His preference for sauce to gravy, why

He kept on plugging at the four aways —
Likewise their yearly frame: the Frinton folk
Who put him up for summer holidays,
And Christmas at his sister's house in Stoke.

But if he stood and watched the frigid wind
Tousling the clouds, lay on the fusty bed
Telling himself that this was home, and grinned,
And shivered, without shaking off the dread

That how we live measures our own nature,
And at his age having no more to show
Than one hired box should make him pretty sure
He warranted no better, I don't know.
— Philip Larkin

The poem, "Mr. Bleaney", is written in a __________ form.
items.explanation: Philip Larkin's 'Mr Bleaney' (written 1955, collected in The Whitsun Weddings, 1964) opens in a dramatic mode with the landlady's direct speech showing the room to a prospective lodger ('This was Mr Bleaney's room...') and the speaker's reply ('I'll take it').
